title: Brother, Can You Spare 1.2 Million?

jokes.text: Hank's 'Miss Saigon' anti-Asian driving joke
jokes.setup: Hank says he was almost killed on the 101, building sympathy for a near-miss story
jokes.punchline: The 'attackers' were the entire cast of Miss Saigon, pivoting immediately into a racist DMV joke about Asian drivers
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's so perfectly calibrated to Hank's oblivious bigotry — he's clearly not a bad person, just an unreconstructed Hollywood blowhard. The 'Miss Saigon' specificity elevates it above a generic racist driver joke because it signals Hank's cultural frame of reference (theater). Still, it relies on an easy stereotype and doesn't subvert itself. Character integration is the strongest element here.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I was almost killed on the way here. I'm on the 101, and all of a sudden the entire cast of miss Saigon comes out of nowhere and tries to sideswipe me.

jokes.text: 'Oh, it's an AIDS thing, right?' / 'No, but it's always an AIDS thing.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Hank to pledge money for a charity walkathon
jokes.punchline: Hank guesses AIDS unprompted, then explains it's not because he knows — it's because charity walkathons are always for AIDS
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical, and genuinely observational. The structure is nearly perfect: a real-seeming clairvoyance is immediately deflated by a meta-cynical explanation. It works as character comedy for Hank (cynical industry insider) but also as pure observational comedy about charity culture in the early 90s. 'It's always an AIDS thing' is a quotable, precise line delivered with total confidence. This is the show's sensibility in one exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: These asians... I mean, they must have a deal with the dmv. They... they keep getting the licenses.

jokes.text: '20 whole dollars. Can a cure be far behind?'
jokes.setup: The walkathon pledger suggests a dollar a mile for 20 miles
jokes.punchline: Hank deadpans that $20 is surely enough to cure the disease
jokes.explanation: Compact, biting, and perfectly Hank. The irony lands because it's delivered with total sincerity — he's not being cruel, he's just genuinely calibrating the cosmic distance between $20 and a cure. Economy is excellent: five words do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, it's an aids thing, right?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, you know about it?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, but it's always an aids thing.

jokes.text: 'It's an awful, horrid disease and I'll... I'll need a receipt.'
jokes.setup: Hank appears to be expressing genuine sympathy for AIDS victims
jokes.punchline: The emotional sincerity is immediately undercut by a request for a tax receipt
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed character joke. The pause before 'I'll need a receipt' is doing heavy lifting — you genuinely think he's about to say something heartfelt. Instead, the punchline reveals that Hank's primary emotional engagement with charitable giving is tax optimization. It's quintessential Hank and quintessential Larry Sanders Show. Could only be this character. Highly quotable and earns rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, how does a dollar a mile sound?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 20 whole dollars. Can a cure be far behind?

jokes.text: Larry immediately escalates the pledge from $20/mile to $25/mile when he learns the cause is AIDS
jokes.setup: Larry asks what the cause is after already agreeing to $20/mile — implying he might retract if he doesn't approve
jokes.punchline: Learning it's AIDS, he immediately ups it to $25, signaling that his generosity is performative and calibrated to optics
jokes.explanation: A perfect contrast to the Hank pledge scene — where Hank is stingy and cynical, Larry is generous but his generosity is immediately revealed as image-management. The callback structure adds resonance. The joke is subtle enough that it rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Happy to. How's 20 bucks a mile?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great. That's $400.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What is the cause, aids? Yeah, make it 25.

jokes.text: 'Beverly, I think it's time we sent that memo out again... the one about people not talking to you first thing in the morning?'
jokes.setup: Larry has just been hit up for charity money before he's fully settled in for the morning
jokes.punchline: He has a standing memo about this — suggesting this happens so regularly he has bureaucratic infrastructure to address it
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Larry's antisocial neurosis is so entrenched it has been codified into workplace policy. Beverly's matter-of-fact confirmation of the memo's existence deepens the absurdity. Good character integration — this is pure Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It'd be nice to get some from a woman occasionally, wouldn't it?

jokes.text: Larry receives fan mail containing men's underwear — and the implication that it's a regular occurrence from the same male sender
jokes.setup: Beverly hands Larry fan mail described as 'tantalizing'
jokes.punchline: It's men's underwear, again, from the same person, and Larry's only complaint is that he wishes he occasionally got some from a woman
jokes.explanation: The escalating beat structure — 'same person?', 'yep yep yep' — and Larry's resigned 'nevertheless...' before looking at the underwear gives this a nice rhythm. The punchline (he'd accept it from women) is the character joke: Larry isn't troubled by the male underwear per se, just the gender ratio.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: A few seconds ago, I saw Meg Ryan's head floating above my credenza.

jokes.text: Artie bursts in claiming to see Meg Ryan's head floating above his credenza due to paint fumes
jokes.setup: Artie staggers in explaining the office was painted, he's loopy from fumes
jokes.punchline: His hallucination is specifically Meg Ryan's disembodied head floating above his credenza
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Meg Ryan's head' is the joke — it's exactly the right celebrity for a late-night TV producer in the mid-90s to hallucinate, and 'floating above my credenza' is a precisely observed detail that grounds the absurdity. Artie's matter-of-fact delivery of this while clearly impaired is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, my... my interior designer's named bryn mawr.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, uh, no, Bob told me he makes a lot more money using that name.

jokes.text: 'No, my interior designer's named Bryn Mawr' / 'Oh, Bob told me he makes a lot more money using that name.' / 'Pretentious prick.'
jokes.setup: Larry is confused when Beverly refers to his interior designer as 'Bob'
jokes.punchline: Bob adopted the pretentious name 'Bryn Mawr' for professional reasons; Larry's verdict: 'Pretentious prick.'
jokes.explanation: A tight three-beat exchange. The reveal is funny (rebranding yourself as a Welsh college for money), and 'pretentious prick' as Larry's immediate judgment — especially given his own name-obsessed world — has a nice ironic undercurrent. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, he said this one is from portugal, so it'll cost you 6,000 extra.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Heh. Iordy, I did some grand humping in portugal. I got a mysterious itch in lisbon.

jokes.text: 'Lordy, I did some grand humping in Portugal. I got a mysterious itch in Lisbon.'
jokes.setup: The conversation is about Portuguese tiles and which one is worth the premium
jokes.punchline: Artie derails into a non-sequitur about sexual conquests and a resultant STI in Lisbon
jokes.explanation: The joke is pure Artie — a man of enormous appetites who can't discuss anything without it triggering a memory of some debauchery. 'Mysterious itch in Lisbon' is a great phrase. Character integration is the strongest element. The structure is loose (it's more of a non-sequitur) but the delivery implied by the text sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, it's getting more and more difficult to pretend you're not here.

jokes.text: 'It's getting more and more difficult to pretend you're not here.'
jokes.setup: Artie asked them to pretend he wasn't there while he recovered from paint fumes; he's been making increasingly disruptive overshares
jokes.punchline: Larry's deadpan acknowledgment that the pretense has become untenable
jokes.explanation: A clean callback punchline to Artie's entrance request. It's economical and dry — exactly one sentence doing exactly the right amount of work. The humor is in the gap between Artie's absurd request and the reality of his behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, let's go with the one from portugal. Because, you know, if I get the cheaper one, then I'm always gonna think there's a better tile in portugal.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You know, it's getting more and more difficult to pretend you're not here.'
jokes.setup: Artie asked everyone to pretend he's not there, then proceeded to dominate the room with TMI anecdotes
jokes.punchline: Larry's exasperated callback to the 'pretend I'm not here' request — perfectly timed, perfectly dry
jokes.explanation: The callback lands because the gap between Artie's request and his behavior is so large. Larry's delivery — stating the obvious with complete weariness — is the classic Larry Sanders straight-man move. Economy is near-perfect: one sentence, maximum exasperation.

dialogue.line: I don't know what you've heard about us, Mr... bobo.

dialogue.speaker: Bobo
dialogue.line: Mr. Bobo.

dialogue.speaker: Bobo
dialogue.line: No, just bobo.

jokes.text: Larry chooses the more expensive Portuguese tile specifically because he fears he'll always wonder if there's a better tile in Portugal
jokes.setup: Larry is told the two tiles look identical but one costs $6,000 more because it's from Portugal
jokes.punchline: He chooses the expensive one not for quality but to avoid the psychological torment of wondering if he missed out — even though he just found out he's broke
jokes.explanation: A genuinely insightful character joke that doubles as psychological comedy. The reasoning is impeccably Larry: paranoid, self-defeating, financially irresponsible, and completely internally consistent. The joke gains enormous retroactive irony when we learn moments later that his checks are bouncing — he's spending $6k extra to avoid FOMO while going broke. High character integration; this joke could not belong to any other character.

dialogue.line: All right, I can see what's going on. You're one of those clowns who's always on.

jokes.text: The clown job interview: interviewer insists 'no need' for clown business, clown immediately starts performing anyway
jokes.setup: An apparently serious job interview is being conducted with someone named 'Bobo' at 'Clown Corps' which 'takes clowning very seriously'
jokes.punchline: The interviewer can't maintain professional distance from someone who is constitutionally incapable of not clowning
jokes.explanation: The sketch-within-a-show concept is funny in concept (a bureaucratic clown corporation) but the execution in transcript form is limited. The comedy relies heavily on physical performance we can't fully access. The self-interruption for the phone call ('Would you hold my calls?') while the clown presumably continues performing is a nice structural beat.

dialogue.line: [Water spraying sound] Oh! There you go. Jesus Christ.

jokes.text: Artie offers the clown something to drink — followed immediately by implied seltzer-to-the-face gag
jokes.setup: Artie, maintaining professionalism, politely offers a drink
jokes.punchline: The clown presumably squirts him or delivers a seltzer gag — inferred from Artie's 'Oh! There you go. Jesus Christ.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Artie's exasperation ('Jesus Christ') is so at odds with his earlier studied professionalism. The physical comedy itself is a classic clown bit — not original — but the framing in a job interview makes it funnier. Without seeing it, it reads as moderate. Probably plays better visually.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is it me, or does this suck?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I mean, I hate this sketch.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah. So do I.

jokes.text: The clown is offered a drink and responds with what is presumably a water-squirting gag
jokes.setup: Interviewer politely offers the clown a drink in the middle of the professional interview
jokes.punchline: 'Oh! There you go. / Jesus Christ. / Is it me, or does this suck?' — the clown has sprayed the interviewer
jokes.explanation: Functional slapstick that works primarily as a visual gag we can only partially infer. 'Is it me, or does this suck?' shifts the meta-commentary — we realize it's a sketch being rehearsed and someone is breaking. The actual spray gag is basic, but the context reveal elevates it slightly.

dialogue.line: You must get laid a lot, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Bobo
dialogue.line: It's the shoe thing, you know? The kick size, dick size.

dialogue.speaker: Bobo
dialogue.line: Yeah, these are bruno maglis size 112.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Is it me, or does this suck? I mean, I hate this sketch.' — then the writer says he agrees, surprising Hank
jokes.setup: Hank complains about the sketch while still in the middle of rehearsing it
jokes.punchline: When the writer immediately agrees 'Yeah. So do I,' Hank's 'What?' reaction reveals he expected pushback, not agreement — his complaint was performative
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is clean — Hank's 'What?' is the laugh. The joke reveals Hank's performative insecurity: he wanted validation, not honesty. Very character-specific. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: How much, Frank?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Uh, a double, I guess, please.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I mean, how much is left?

jokes.text: The clown tells Hank: 'You must get laid a lot, huh? It's the shoe thing, you know? The kick size, dick size.' / 'Yeah, these are Bruno Magli size 112.'
jokes.setup: After the sketch ends, the clown makes small talk with Hank about his enormous shoes
jokes.punchline: The clown implies Hank has an enormous penis based on shoe size; Hank responds with gleeful, specific confirmation — and name-drops Bruno Magli shoes (a O.J. Simpson reference current in 1995)
jokes.explanation: The Bruno Magli reference would have been electrically topical in 1995 (the O.J. Simpson trial was ongoing — those were the shoes at the crime scene). Hank's oblivious/gleeful confirmation of his own sexual prowess based on clown-shoe logic is perfectly in character. The topical reference adds a rewatch dimension for period viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I told you that it would like this in the fourth quarter.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, I did. L... when we were at the Ivy...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: no.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I warned you when you were...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: yes, when you were tipping the valet.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, you didn't.

jokes.text: Frank's escalating financial revelations: 'I'm responsible because I own the company, but I didn't have anything to do with this'
jokes.setup: Frank is in Larry's office explaining the financial disaster
jokes.punchline: He opens by claiming full technical responsibility while simultaneously disclaiming any actual involvement
jokes.explanation: A recognizable form of corporate/professional weaseling rendered in miniature. The contradiction is stated so baldly it becomes funny. Not a huge laugh but solid cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I don't drink.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, you just asked me for a drink.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I don't think that's the case.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You just asked me for a drink.

jokes.text: Frank asks for a drink mid-confrontation; when Larry asks 'how much is left?', Frank thinks he means the size of the pour
jokes.setup: Larry asks 'How much, Frank?' after the revelation of financial mismanagement
jokes.punchline: Frank hears this as a drink order — 'A double, I guess, please' — before Larry clarifies he means how much money is left
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection executed with good economy. The audience understands Larry's meaning instantly, making Frank's misread both reveal his state of mind (he needs a drink to face what's coming) and provide a beat of comic relief before the real blow lands. Well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Are you an idiot? Answer me. Answer me, you stupid shit. Are you an idiot? / Get the fuck out of the office!

jokes.text: Frank insists he warned Larry 'when you were tipping the valet' at the Ivy — a claim Larry denies
jokes.setup: Frank claims he warned Larry about the financial situation at dinner; Larry says he never mentioned it
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'warning' was delivered at the precise moment Larry was distracted tipping a valet — the comedy of a catastrophic disclosure timed to guarantee non-reception
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'when you were tipping the valet' is what makes this land. It's a perfectly observed piece of L.A. life — the moment of valet-tipping is a known social distraction — and Frank's passive CYA behavior (informing you when you can't possibly process it) is a recognizable type. Solid cringe comedy with good industry-insider texture.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What the fuck's the matter with him today?

jokes.text: 'You're editing your memory.' / 'How long have you been drinking, Frank?' / 'I don't drink.' / 'You just asked me for a drink.' / 'I don't think that's the case.'
jokes.setup: Frank tells Larry he's 'editing his memory' about not being warned; Larry counters by accusing Frank of drinking
jokes.punchline: Frank denies drinking despite having just asked for a drink thirty seconds earlier, then denies that too
jokes.explanation: A tight callback that escalates Frank's unreliability as a narrator. The move from 'I don't drink' to 'I don't think that's the case' (re: having just asked for a drink) is beautifully specific. It mirrors the episode's theme of financial denial with Frank's personal denial. 'I don't think that's the case' is a great line — the passive voice of a man gaslighting in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's been over 3 hours, and the man hasn't moved a muscle. Something tells me we won't be doing a show tonight.

jokes.text: 'Everything is under control.' / 'Everything is under control? You have the nerve to come in here and tell me everything's under control when I'm fucking broke?'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to reassure Larry that everything is under control
jokes.punchline: Larry's explosion — the repetition of 'everything is under control' as accusation rather than reassurance
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from Larry's escalating fury and the absolute wrongness of Frank's platitude in context. Not the sharpest joke in the episode but the emotion is earned and the explosion feels good. The repetition of the phrase as both reassurance and accusation is effective.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Between my fucking ex-wife and the... and the ponies, I'm lucky if I can swing postage.

jokes.text: Staff member outside the office: 'What the fuck's the matter with him today?'
jokes.setup: Larry has just screamed and thrown Frank out of his office in a volcanic rage
jokes.punchline: A bystander's reaction treats this apparently as a variation from Larry's normal behavior, implying this kind of outburst is familiar enough to be contextualized
jokes.explanation: A quick button on the Frank confrontation. Works as a world-building joke — Larry's volatility is normalized in his workplace environment. The 'today' implies there's a daily baseline of Larry-chaos that this exceeded. Economy is the joke's best feature.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're gonna be wiping your ass with $100 bills.

jokes.text: Larry has been lying under a pillow for 3+ hours without moving — it's now close to showtime
jokes.setup: Beverly and Artie are outside Larry's room; apparently Larry is in some kind of stupor
jokes.punchline: He's been motionless under a pillow for over 3 hours with showtime approaching
jokes.explanation: A great piece of Larry character comedy — his emotional collapses are apparently so total that the pillow-over-the-head withdrawal is a known coping mechanism. The time detail (3+ hours) and the proximity to showtime creates absurdist dramatic irony. The visual of an adult television host lying motionless under a pillow is funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You fucker. Don't ever do that to me again.

jokes.text: 'I know how to get him out of there. I hate to do it.' [PAUSE] 'I have no choice.'
jokes.setup: Artie declares he knows how to get Larry out of his stupor but dreads the method
jokes.punchline: The method turns out to be... Hank. Sending in the most annoying person they know as a form of shock therapy.
jokes.explanation: The pause between 'I hate to do it' and 'I have no choice' does comedic work — it implies something drastic, perhaps violent. The reveal that the last resort is Hank is the punchline: Artie deploying Hank as an irritant weapon. This establishes Artie's relationship to Hank economically and amusingly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll go over there and bounce that little fucker out the window.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What? Ha ha. Just kidding.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know, but I do know a couple of guys who can be helpful... one quick phone call.

jokes.text: Hank's 'sympathetic' visit: 'Not that I'm rolling in it. Between my fucking ex-wife and the ponies, I'm lucky if I can swing postage.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to comfort Larry about his financial ruin by offering money
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies that he himself is nearly broke — gambling losses and an ex-wife have left him barely able to afford stamps
jokes.explanation: Hank's offer of financial support is undercut immediately by the revelation that he can barely afford postage. 'Ex-wife and the ponies' is a great character shorthand — it tells you everything about Hank in five words. The pathos of his 'help' offer is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I fired my accountant this week because evidently, he invested my money in a company that had plans to install tampon dispensers at the citadel.

jokes.text: Hank's endorsement pep talk: 'Your name and your likeness... a couple of major endorsement deals... you're gonna be wiping your ass with $100 bills.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to cheer Larry up, pivoting from 'I have no money to give you' to 'here's my advice'
jokes.punchline: His financial advice culminates in the specific image of Larry wiping his ass with $100 bills
jokes.explanation: The vulgarity of the specific image ('wiping your ass') is a Hank signature — he's trying to be encouraging and inspirational and lands on bathroom imagery. Mildly funny, mostly as character texture. The advice itself is reasonably sound, which makes the landing image even more deflating.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just found out my accountant has a 3-tiered system, actually, win, place, and show.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I know what you need... [pause] You need a hug.'
jokes.setup: After the pep talk fails to rouse Larry, Hank pauses dramatically
jokes.punchline: The solution to a man's financial ruin, arrived at with great seriousness, is a hug
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'You need a hug' does significant comic work — it promises something profound and delivers something both sincere and absurd. The subsequent 'Don't resist. Give in. There you go.' is Hank at his most weirdly earnest. The joke is in Hank's complete comfort with the hug as problem-solving.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: And about the walkathon, you don't have to feel obligated to...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Paula, come on. I'm not destitute, for God's sake.

jokes.text: Larry, finally roused from depression by Hank's forcible hug: 'You fucker. Don't ever do that to me again.' Artie: 'It was showtime. My hands were tied.'
jokes.setup: The hug works — Larry is snapped out of his stupor
jokes.punchline: Larry's furious 'You fucker' response, and Artie's immediate pragmatic 'It was showtime. My hands were tied.' — as if deploying Hank for a forced hug was a legitimate production decision
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the 'send Hank in' plan is excellent. Artie's 'It was showtime. My hands were tied.' is a great line — it frames a forced hug as a regrettable but necessary production choice. The callback lands, the character voices are all perfectly distinct, and the rhythm of the exchange is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: How much was it?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: I think it was 25 doll... you know what? It was $10 a mile.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: It was $5.00 a mile.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If it's $5.00 a mile, that's fine.

jokes.text: Artie offers to 'bounce Frank out the window' then: 'Just kidding. But I do know a couple of guys who can be helpful... one quick phone call.'
jokes.setup: Larry says he has a plan for dealing with Frank; Artie immediately escalates to violence
jokes.punchline: He walks back 'bounce him out the window' as a joke, but then immediately replaces it with an offer to make a call — implying actual mob connections
jokes.explanation: Artie's implied mob connections are a running undercurrent in the show. The joke's structure — 'just kidding' immediately undercut by 'but I know a couple of guys' — is perfect. The 'expense?' offer adds a capper. Larry's refusal and Artie's confused response ('Oh hell, what is it, the expense?') deepens Artie's character as someone for whom this is genuinely not a big deal.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That would be your uncle?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Yeah. That's right. Ah. Mm-hmm.

jokes.text: The show's on-air 'thank you' sequence — Larry performing his host persona seamlessly after the Frank crisis
jokes.setup: Larry has just come out from under a pillow after a three-hour breakdown about being broke
jokes.punchline: Cut directly to him smiling and performing his charming host act for the audience, the crisis invisible
jokes.explanation: The structural irony of this transition is strong — it's the show commenting on the performer's ability to compartmentalize. The audience (in the show) has no idea what just happened. This is meta-commentary on the nature of live television performance and works as a visual irony joke even without dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. Listen, this doesn't have a happy ending, does it, Phil?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: No. I'm sorry.

jokes.text: Larry's stand-up: 'I fired my accountant this week because evidently he invested my money in a company that had plans to install tampon dispensers at the Citadel.'
jokes.setup: Larry announces he fired his accountant
jokes.punchline: The investment was in tampon dispensers at the Citadel (a military school that had just lost a landmark case about admitting women)
jokes.explanation: A sharp, topical joke that works on multiple levels: it's economical, the Citadel reference was extremely current (Shannon Faulkner had just been admitted and immediately withdrew in 1995), and the absurdity of the investment is perfectly calibrated. The joke works independently of the topical reference but is sharpened by it. For stand-up, this is genuinely well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: God, I suck at cheering people up.

jokes.text: 'My accountant has a 3-tiered system: win, place, and show.'
jokes.setup: Larry explains his accountant's investment methodology
jokes.punchline: The 'system' is horse-racing betting terminology — the accountant is literally gambling with client money
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical stand-up — eight words that convey the entire joke with no waste. The 'win, place, and show' delivers the punchline precisely while doubling as a legitimate description of the accountant's financial 'philosophy.' High quotability. For stand-up this is an above-average joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: We got him back for you. We nailed him. The two us, Artie and me. That little cocksucker Frank is down. It was beautiful.

jokes.text: 'He's been recognized by the government and arrested.'
jokes.setup: Larry says his accountant has just been 'recognized by the government'
jokes.punchline: '...and arrested' — the phrase 'recognized by the government' is recontextualized from an honor to a legal action
jokes.explanation: A textbook misdirection/wordplay joke. The phrase 'recognized by the government' carries two meanings, and the pause before 'and arrested' pivots perfectly. Economy is excellent. Not particularly deep but very efficiently constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's a trellis. It's a trellis. / And this trellis... this is a gorgeous trellis. It's just... just gorgeous. And we stood there. We admired it for quite a while. Then I burned it down.

jokes.text: Artie's reaction to Larry's plan: 'That's your plan for taking care of Frank? A little gentle ribbing, a couple of jokes you hope he'll see?'
jokes.setup: Larry's 'plan' to address Frank is revealed to be: do jokes about the situation on his show
jokes.punchline: Artie's incredulous summary — 'jokes you hope he'll see' — deflates the plan completely
jokes.explanation: This is the punchline to the entire stand-up sequence — we now understand that the on-air jokes weren't just comedy, they were Larry's 'plan.' Artie's reaction is perfect: matter-of-fact disbelief that this constitutes a plan. His follow-up ('I'm going home now... I have to work in the morning') deepens the comedy by showing his contempt while also being genuinely reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Ha! Not now there ain't.

jokes.text: 'I'm going home now. I'm getting a good night's sleep. You know why? Because I have to work in the morning.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just absorbed Larry's non-plan of joke-based revenge
jokes.punchline: He simply announces he's going home like a man clocking out after a long day, completely deflating any remaining dramatic tension
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Artie — a man who has seen everything, tried everything, and knows when to cut his losses. The normality of 'I have to work in the morning' against the backdrop of financial ruin and schemes of revenge is perfectly deflating. The joke is in Artie's complete pragmatic sanity in an insane situation. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: There's no trellis at his new house. There's a trellis at his old house... not at his new house... the one on Benedict canyon that he just moved into.

jokes.text: Paula walks-back the walkathon pledge amount in front of Larry: $25 becomes $10, then $5
jokes.setup: Paula approaches Larry after his show about the walkathon, saying he doesn't have to feel obligated after learning about his money situation
jokes.punchline: As Larry insists he's fine and asks the amount, Paula downwardly revises the pledge in real time: $25 → $10 → $5
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback that subverts the episode's opening. In the cold open, Larry casually bumped the pledge up for AIDS; now, with his finances exposed, Paula is quietly lowering it in front of him while he maintains dignity. Larry's insistence ('I'm not destitute, for God's sake') while watching the number drop is perfectly observed awkward comedy. The $5/mile = $100 total tag is a precise, satisfying button. One of the episode's best structural jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, when that asian woman came out of the house screaming, I just thought she was the housekeeper.

jokes.text: Phil's dead-end sympathy story: his uncle's farm supply business went belly up, 'and he was a really great guy.' / 'This doesn't have a happy ending, does it, Phil?'
jokes.setup: Phil tries to comfort Larry with a parallel story about his uncle
jokes.punchline: Larry interrupts to confirm the story has no redemptive arc — and Phil admits it doesn't
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully constructed piece of awkward comedy. Larry's interruption is both a character reveal (he recognizes a bad-news story mid-telling) and perfectly structured — 'This doesn't have a happy ending, does it, Phil?' anticipates the audience's realization simultaneously with Larry's. Phil's simple 'No' is perfect. Then 'God, I suck at cheering people up' is a lovely self-aware button. High economy and strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: 9 shows a night, every half hour. You know, it's like vaudeville days.

jokes.text: 'God, I suck at cheering people up.'
jokes.setup: Phil has just confirmed his sympathy story had no happy ending
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges his own failure at the very task he was attempting with total equanimity
jokes.explanation: Six words, maximum economy, and a perfectly self-aware button on the Phil-Larry scene. The joke is that Phil has no follow-up plan — he just apologies and leaves. Larry's 'Mm-hmm' acceptance of this is the implied reaction that completes the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is the car gonna be a compact, also?

jokes.text: 'That would be your uncle?' (in response to Phil's 'my dad's brother')
jokes.setup: Phil explains the story is about 'my dad's brother'
jokes.punchline: Larry dryly notes that this is, in fact, the definition of an uncle
jokes.explanation: A classic Larry Sanders 'straight man points out the obvious' beat. Larry's inability to let even small conversational imprecisions go — especially while in an emotional crisis — is a neat character reveal. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I like it. / I like it. Hot in the summer. Heh.

jokes.text: Beverly forgot to send the memo — again — and Larry discovers this mid-conversation with Phil about the memo
jokes.setup: Larry references the memo to shut down Phil, then realizes Beverly never sent it
jokes.punchline: Beverly apologizes — 'Oh, I forgot. I'm sorry, Larry. L... I forgot.' — the memo about not bothering Larry was itself forgotten, meaning Larry gets bothered
jokes.explanation: Nicely closes the memo running gag loop — the tool Larry deploys to avoid human contact keeps failing to deploy because the person responsible for deploying it is human. Circular and satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I got a drinking problem. For the last 2 years, I've been off and on antidepressants. I hate my life, Larry.

jokes.text: Larry walks up to his agent's meeting in progress and won't be told who it's with — 'I would like to know who he's in a meeting with and I would like to talk to him'
jokes.setup: Beverly tells Larry his agent Stevie will call after his meeting; Larry immediately wants to know who Stevie is meeting with
jokes.punchline: The comedic tension of a major star demanding to know exactly what their agent is doing at any given moment — the paranoia and control issues on full display
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. Larry's paranoia about his agent's other clients is on-brand, but this beat doesn't have a clear punchline — it's more setup for the Stevie call. Works as texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So this is 5% of what I lost?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, more or less.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Where's the rest?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, I'm working on it, man.

jokes.text: 'Come on, last one in has to drop trou.'
jokes.setup: Artie and another character are leading Larry into his office with news
jokes.punchline: Artie's attempt to generate excitement involves the threat of pants removal
jokes.explanation: A brief Artie non-sequitur that works purely as character texture. The casual invocation of 'drop trou' as a motivational tool is absurdly Artie. Not a big joke but it colors his character.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: But for now... we're square, right?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What do you mean, we're square, Frank?

jokes.text: The trellis-burning story: Artie and Hank went to the wrong house (Frank's old house) and burned down a stranger's trellis
jokes.setup: Artie and Hank reveal they took revenge on Frank by going to his house and burning his trellis
jokes.punchline: Hank reveals there's no trellis at Frank's new house — they burned down the trellis at Frank's OLD house (a stranger's property)
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak. The setup takes considerable time (Artie describing the trellis with admiration, 'we admired it for quite a while, then I burned it down'), which makes the delayed reveal of the error devastating. Hank's casual 'Ha! Not now there ain't' followed by 'There's no trellis at his new house' is a masterclass in comic timing. The structure is near-perfect: they solve the wrong problem with maximum commitment. This approaches the show's best work — it's character comedy (Artie has lighter fluid in his trunk as a matter of course; Hank's navigational incompetence), escalation, and absurdism simultaneously. 'Nice going, you fucking moron' as Artie's response to Hank is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: These are the chins. Uh, edward and allison. And edward's mother, whose name I'm not gonna even try to pronounce.

jokes.text: Artie's trellis appreciation speech: 'This is a gorgeous trellis. It's just... just gorgeous. And we stood there. We admired it for quite a while. Then I burned it down.'
jokes.setup: Artie is building to the revenge act
jokes.punchline: The loving description of the trellis's beauty is immediately followed by its destruction — 'Then I burned it down' delivered as a non-event
jokes.explanation: This is the single best line in the episode and one of the best lines in the series. The structure is almost mathematically perfect: a tender, specific aesthetic appreciation ('just gorgeous') followed by the most casual act of arson imaginable. 'Then I burned it down' has no preamble, no emotional escalation, no justification — it simply follows. The total absence of dramatic weight is the joke. Only Artie could deliver this: a man of culture, taste, and absolutely no moral hesitation. This approaches the 9.5 anchor on the calibration scale. Highly quotable, rewatch-essential, character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm so sorry about the Margaret cho show.

jokes.text: 'There's no trellis at his new house... the one on Benedict Canyon that he just moved into.' / 'Oh, shit.' / 'Nice going, you fucking moron.'
jokes.setup: Artie has been proudly narrating the trellis burning; Hank realizes the error
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'nice going, you fucking moron' directed at Hank — who was his co-conspirator — is the cherry on top
jokes.explanation: The punchline to the entire trellis sequence. Artie blaming Hank for a plan that Artie executed is a perfect inversion of responsibility — classic character comedy. 'Nice going, you fucking moron' works because Artie is the one who 'ran with it' (his own words). The escalating 'oh shit' reactions from Larry are the straight-man beat that lands the comedy. Works in tandem with joke #46 and #47 as a suite.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Then let's go with the cheaper one because, uh, why waste the money?

jokes.text: 'You know, when that Asian woman came out of the house screaming, I just thought she was the housekeeper.'
jokes.setup: In the chaos of realizing they burned the wrong trellis, Hank adds a detail
jokes.punchline: A screaming woman emerged during the arson, and Hank's in-the-moment interpretation was that she was the housekeeper — revealing the depth of his assumptions
jokes.explanation: A devastating callback to Hank's opening racist joke, now given terrible context. The callback is thematically loaded: Hank's assumptions about Asian people (from the Miss Saigon driving joke) are now revealed to have had real consequences — his assumption that an Asian woman was 'the housekeeper' meant he didn't register the homeowner fleeing from the arson he was committing. The show doesn't comment on this; it lets the horror speak for itself. This is the dark underbelly of Hank's casual bigotry made manifest. High character integration and a rewatch essential.

dialogue.line: Apparently, some nut drove up on the sidewalk and ran over his foot.

jokes.text: Stevie's pitch call: 'Kentucky Fried Chicken. What does that mean? Spokesman. You. One year.'
jokes.setup: Larry calls his agent needing money fast
jokes.punchline: Stevie's first offer is KFC spokesperson — Larry's rebranding from sophistication to fried chicken is the implicit joke
jokes.explanation: Good Hollywood satire — the gap between a talk-show host's self-image and the commercial work available is the joke. Larry's immediate 'So I'm the new Colonel Sanders?' shows his grasp of what's being offered. Stevie's 'Ha! Funny. I'll pitch that.' is a nice agent-speaks beat.

jokes.text: 'So I'm the new Colonel Sanders?' / 'Ha! Funny. I'll pitch that.'
jokes.setup: Larry quips about being 'Colonel Sanders' as the KFC spokesperson
jokes.punchline: Stevie takes it literally and says he'll actually pitch it — an agent's reflex to monetize any idea, even a throwaway joke
jokes.explanation: A sharp agent-character joke. The irony is that Stevie's 'Ha! Funny. I'll pitch that.' simultaneously dismisses the joke AND takes it seriously — an agent's worldview where everything is pitchable. This is specific showbiz satire.

jokes.text: 'Hey, take this the right way, but I wish you'd go broke every day.'
jokes.setup: Stevie is pitching multiple revenue streams for Larry after the financial crisis
jokes.punchline: He expresses that Larry's financial desperation is professionally useful — making him easier to sell and more willing to do anything
jokes.explanation: 'Take this the right way' is a perfect setup — it signals something inappropriate is coming. The line itself is a precise, honest articulation of the agent-client relationship that's rarely stated so baldly: clients are most profitable when desperate. High quotability, strong character integration (only a confident, mercenary agent says this), and earned rather than cheap.

jokes.text: Lindsay Wagner needed 'one of the trucks' to cart her Ford payment home
jokes.setup: Stevie brags about Lindsay Wagner's Ford deal to contextualize what he can get Larry
jokes.punchline: The payment was so enormous she needed a Ford truck to transport it
jokes.explanation: A solid agent-bragging joke. The image of Lindsay Wagner loading cash into a Ford truck is absurdist but grounded. The meta-irony (the Ford commercial pays for a Ford truck) adds a layer. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: 'Caesar's or MGM?' / 'Whichever one pays more.' / 'How about both? 9 shows a night, every half hour. It's like the vaudeville days.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks to book a Vegas residency
jokes.punchline: Stevie escalates to 9 shows a night, every half hour — an absurd volume that references vaudeville-era exploitation of performers
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat — Stevie's enthusiasm for Larry's desperate situation leads him to overbook with comic specificity. '9 shows a night, every half hour' is a precise absurdity that works. The vaudeville reference adds historical texture to the industry satire.

jokes.text: The Lexus executive asks Larry to read the copy standing up 'like you would if you were actually doing the commercial'; Artie: 'I'll be the camera, and the coffee table's the car.'
jokes.setup: A formal Lexus pitch meeting is happening; the executive wants to workshop the copy in the room
jokes.punchline: Artie's offer to play 'the camera' while treating the coffee table as the car reduces the corporate pitch to children's play
jokes.explanation: Artie's gleeful sabotage of a formal business meeting by turning it into an improv exercise is perfectly in character. The contrast between the executive's corporate formality and Artie's chaos is good cringe comedy.

jokes.text: 'Is the car gonna be a compact, also?' (Larry about Artie the 'camera' sitting small next to the coffee-table 'car')
jokes.setup: Artie has designated himself as the camera and the coffee table as the car
jokes.punchline: Larry notes the physical incongruity — the 'car' (a small coffee table) and the 'camera' (Artie crouching) create a miniature diorama
jokes.explanation: A quick visual joke inference from the scene — Larry's dry observation punctures the absurdity of the setup. Economy is the strength. Works better in visual form but reads well in transcript.

jokes.text: The leather interior exchange: 'The leather interior? How do you feel about it?... Does it make you feel good? Do you like it?' / 'I like it.' / 'Hot in the summer. Heh.'
jokes.setup: The Lexus executive pauses mid-copy reading to probe Larry's emotional relationship with leather upholstery
jokes.punchline: Larry's authentic response — 'Hot in the summer' — is the opposite of the 'profound emotional response' required
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed piece of showbiz cringe comedy. The executive's instructions — 'love the leather... have a profound emotional response' — are themselves funny (the commodification of emotion in advertising), but Larry's totally honest 'Hot in the summer' is the perfect punchline. It's what everyone actually thinks about leather seats. Larry's inability to perform enthusiasm he doesn't feel, even when his financial life depends on it, is quintessential character comedy. 'That's what I thought' from the executive is a deadpan horror button.

jokes.text: 'That's what I thought.' (Executive's reaction to 'Hot in the summer')
jokes.setup: The executive has asked Larry to have a 'profound emotional response' to leather; Larry says it's 'hot in the summer'
jokes.punchline: 'That's what I thought' — delivered flatly, signaling the executive knew this wasn't going to work
jokes.explanation: Three words that carry enormous weight as a reaction beat. The executive has seen this before — celebrities who can't fake it. 'That's what I thought' is resignation masquerading as professionalism. Economy is almost perfect.

jokes.text: Frank shows up at Larry's home late at night to confess: drinking problem, antidepressants, 'I hate my life, Larry. I hate being a fucking accountant.'
jokes.setup: Frank arrives uninvited at night, apparently seeking reconciliation
jokes.punchline: Instead of a plan to make Larry whole, he delivers an extended personal crisis confession — using his destruction of Larry's finances as an occasion for his own catharsis
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy about the audacity of making your victim listen to your problems. 'I hate being a fucking accountant' as the reason for losing millions of dollars is a reductio ad absurdum of professional accountability. Larry's 'Uh-huh' and 'Oh, really?' responses are perfectly calibrated passive hostility.

jokes.text: Frank gives Larry money in an envelope — 'but it's your fees from over the years... I obviously didn't earn 'em. So this is 5% of what I lost?' / 'Well, more or less.'
jokes.setup: Frank offers Larry an envelope of money as repayment
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant calculation that this represents roughly 5% of what he lost, and Frank's breezy 'more or less' confirmation
jokes.explanation: Larry's precise financial calibration ('So this is 5% of what I lost?') and Frank's cheerful 'more or less' is darkly funny. The gap between Frank's sense of gesture and the actual numbers is the joke.

jokes.text: Frank returns Larry's fees — 'It's your fees from over the years, all right? I obviously didn't earn 'em.' Larry: 'So this is 5% of what I lost?' Frank: 'Well, more or less.'
jokes.setup: Frank presents an envelope of cash as his attempt to make things right
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'So this is 5% of what I lost?' — and Frank's confirmation ('more or less') — reveals the envelope contains a trivial fraction of the damage
jokes.explanation: The '5% of what I lost' line is a sharp, economical summary of the absurdity of Frank's gesture. 'More or less' as confirmation is perfectly deadpan. Good comic exchange.

jokes.text: 'But for now... we're square, right?' (Frank to Larry after returning 5% of the money he lost)
jokes.setup: Frank has returned a small portion of the money he lost and confessed his personal problems
jokes.punchline: He asks if they're 'square' — an extraordinary overreach given the circumstances
jokes.explanation: 'We're square, right?' after returning 5% of the money is the ultimate audacity. The line works as dark comedy because Frank seems to genuinely believe the confession plus the partial repayment equals emotional closure. It's a precise observation about a certain type of person.

jokes.text: Frank reveals someone set fire to his old house and says 'I got the message' — Larry denies any knowledge
jokes.setup: Frank mentions someone burned down his (old) house's trellis and he knows it was a message
jokes.punchline: Larry swears he knows nothing about it — while the audience knows exactly what happened, and that the message was delivered to the WRONG house
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly structured irony joke. Frank thinks the arson was a deliberate message from Larry. Larry sincerely denies it. The audience knows the truth — it was an accidental arson on the wrong property that Frank happens to have ALSO owned. Frank has received a 'message' that was never intended for him, interpreted it correctly in spirit, and Larry's denial is technically true but functionally false. The layers of dramatic irony here are exceptional. Earns high marks for structure, earned comedy, and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Larry introduces the Chin family to his staff — the victims of the accidental trellis burning — as people 'whose home was vandalized a few days ago'
jokes.setup: Larry has invited the family whose trellis was burned (accidentally, by Artie and Hank) for a backstage tour as an act of charity
jokes.punchline: Larry is hosting the victims of the crime he (sort of) commissioned while being completely unaware of the connection
jokes.explanation: A beautiful dark comedy payoff. The wrong house belonged to an Asian family (the Chins), which also loops back to Hank's opening Asian-driver joke AND his 'I thought she was the housekeeper' line. The layers of irony compound: Larry is being charitable to people his team accidentally victimized while trying to menace someone else. Artie's visible discomfort is the implied reaction beat.

jokes.text: 'I'm so sorry about the Margaret Cho show.'
jokes.setup: Larry is expressing sympathy to the Chin family about their trellis being burned
jokes.punchline: He pivots from the arson sympathy to an industry reference — apologizing for the cancellation of Margaret Cho's show 'All-American Girl' as if it's a comparable misfortune
jokes.explanation: This is arguably the episode's single most precise joke. The Margaret Cho show ('All-American Girl') had just been cancelled in 1995 after ABC demanded Cho lose weight and made her character 'less Asian.' Larry's apology for this to an Asian family — as if it's personally his fault or equally worth apologizing for — is a stunning compression of Hollywood's racism, talk-show host obliviousness, and Larry's specific brand of tone-deaf sympathy. It also quietly underlines that Larry equates Asian identity with one cultural reference point. The joke is dense with meaning, perfectly economical, and devastatingly specific to the moment. Among the episode's very best.

jokes.text: Larry reverses his tile decision — this time choosing the CHEAPER one — immediately after the financial crisis
jokes.setup: A callback to the Portugal tile decision; Larry is now reconsidering
jokes.punchline: 'They look identical, right?' / 'Yes.' / 'Then let's go with the cheaper one because, uh, why waste the money?' — the exact opposite reasoning of his first decision
jokes.explanation: A structurally perfect callback that completes the episode's thematic arc. In act one, Larry chose the $6,000 more-expensive tile to avoid FOMO. Now, in act three, he makes the exact same decision ('they look identical') with opposite logic ('why waste the money?'). The joke is that both decisions are equally arbitrary and rational-sounding, just reversed. It's the best structural use of callbacks in the episode — not just a reference, but a character-revealing mirror that shows what money does to perspective. The delivery 'Good thinking' from Beverly echoes the first scene perfectly.

jokes.text: Frank has been run over by 'some nut who drove up on the sidewalk'
jokes.setup: Larry has just gotten confirmation that his 'plan' (the jokes) is working — Frank returned money
jokes.punchline: Beverly reports Frank is at Cedars-Sinai — someone drove up on the sidewalk and ran over his foot; the implication being that Artie's 'one quick phone call' was made after all
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke and one of its best. The structure is essentially a two-act story: Artie offers to 'know a couple of guys'; Larry says don't; 'my plan is working'; Frank is in the hospital with a crushed foot from a 'random' driver. The comedy is in what's left unsaid — the show never confirms Artie made the call. It doesn't need to. The dramatic irony is that Larry's smug 'my adult plan is working' is immediately followed by evidence that Artie's plan ALSO worked. The episode ends on a note of perfectly calibrated dark comedy: a broken foot is the sitcom-safe mob punishment. Artie's character is perfectly captured — he does what he said he'd do, quietly, while letting Larry think otherwise. Exceptional structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Frank's 'plan is working' — he got his money back and Frank was scared enough to return fees; Artie drily congratulates Larry on his 'adult' plan
jokes.setup: Larry confirms Frank returned some money; Artie and Hank congratulate him on his plan
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'plan' — some gentle stand-up jokes — is credited with getting results, while the actual catalyst (the wrong-house arson) goes unmentioned by everyone
jokes.explanation: The irony is in what's unsaid — the actual reason Frank returned money was the arson threat (as he explicitly said at the door), not the stand-up jokes. Larry taking credit for the 'adult plan' while the real cause was his friends committing arson at the wrong house is a satisfying comic resolution.

tmdb_overview: Larry scrambles to make some money after his accountant admits he's lost all of Larry's funds. Artie and Hank set out to teach the guy a lesson.
